entry.title: Rethinking Talent, Learning, and AI: Insights from Anil Kumar
entry.content:
In a rapidly evolving business landscape shaped by artificial intelligence, the traditional rules of learning and talent development are being rewritten. In a recent podcast conversation with Anil Kumar, Professor of Business Analytics at Texas A&M University Commerce, a compelling narrative emerged—one that challenges organizations, educators, and professionals to rethink how they approach skills, hiring, and innovation in the age of generative AI. 🚀

AI in the Classroom: The Two Camps 🤖

Generative AI is already deeply embedded in the academic experience. According to Anil Kumar, students today fall into two distinct camps—those who leverage AI to accelerate learning and those who risk over-reliance, potentially weakening critical thinking. This “spectrum of use” highlights a broader truth: AI’s value depends entirely on how it is applied.

Interestingly, today’s students are “AI natives,” seamlessly integrating tools like ChatGPT or Google’s NotebookLM into their daily workflows. Unlike previous generations who had to adapt to digital tools, these students treat AI as an extension of their thinking process. This shift presents both an opportunity and a challenge for educators and employers alike. 🎓

From Usage to Mastery: Teaching Critical Thinking with AI 🧠

Rather than resisting AI, forward-thinking educators are designing curricula that embrace it. In Anil Kumar’s classroom, AI use is not optional—it’s required. However, the emphasis is not on output but on judgment. Students must submit AI-generated responses alongside their own analysis, demonstrating how they refine, critique, and improve upon machine outputs.

This approach flips the narrative. Instead of AI replacing thinking, it becomes a catalyst for deeper reasoning. The goal is to “reverse engineer critical thinking,” ensuring students remain active participants in the learning process rather than passive consumers. 💡

The Skills That Matter Now (and Always) 🔑

Despite the technological shift, some fundamentals remain unchanged. Problem-solving, creativity, curiosity, communication, and critical thinking continue to be indispensable. However, one new competency stands out: AI fluency.

AI fluency doesn’t mean technical mastery—it means understanding the landscape, knowing when and how to use AI tools, and recognizing their limitations. As Anil Kumar emphasizes, professionals don’t need to be experts, but they must be conversant. In a world where AI is ubiquitous, ignorance is no longer an option. 📊

A Broken Hiring Model? Time for Reinvention 🏗️

One of the most provocative insights from the discussion centers on hiring practices. Today’s recruitment process often involves AI-generated job descriptions being evaluated against AI-optimized resumes—a system where “bots are evaluating bots.” The human element, ironically, is diminished.

This raises a critical question: Are organizations overlooking true potential?

Anil Kumar suggests a paradigm shift—moving away from static resumes toward dynamic “artifacts.” These could be digital portfolios, projects, or real-world solutions that showcase a candidate’s journey and capabilities over time. Such artifacts provide a richer, more authentic view of talent than traditional credentials ever could. 📁

The Rise of the Builder Mindset 🛠️

A recurring theme is the power of creation. Whether it’s a high school student building a housing platform or an English major training engineers in AI prompt design, success increasingly belongs to those who can identify problems and build solutions—regardless of formal training.

This “builder mindset” thrives on curiosity and observation. It challenges the notion that only elite institutions produce innovation. Instead, it democratizes creativity, empowering individuals to leverage accessible tools and make meaningful contributions. 🌍

Bridging the Gap: What Organizations Can Do 🤝

For companies—particularly those navigating procurement, technology, or sourcing—the implications are significant. Traditional engagement models with universities (career fairs, internships) may no longer suffice.

Anil Kumar առաջարկs a more continuous, mentorship-driven approach. Imagine professionals mentoring students throughout their academic journey, reviewing their projects, and offering feedback. This not only builds stronger talent pipelines but also ensures alignment between academic preparation and industry needs.

Such a shift requires minimal time investment but delivers high impact—creating a feedback loop that benefits both students and organizations. 📈

The Bigger Picture: Opportunity vs. Inaction 🌟

The overarching message is clear: opportunities in AI and business transformation are vast, but they are not guaranteed. Organizations must actively seek, recognize, and act on them. History has shown that ignoring emerging trends—like Blockbuster did with Netflix—can have lasting consequences.

The future of business is not just about digital transformation; it’s about talent transformation. Those who embrace change, remain curious, and challenge conventional thinking will lead the way. 🔮

entry.title: The Procurement Monthly - August 2026
entry.content:
Summary

Data drawn from the Hackett Group, Ardent Partners, , WorldCC, BCG,  Foundry, SMARTnership, and others, converge on a shared concern: the gap between intention and execution is widening, and it is widening fast. AI is moving from pilot to production, yet 57% of procurement organisations cite data problems as their primary barrier to deploying it well. Sixty-one percent of CPOs see AI primarily as a productivity enabler, yet only 13% of teams operate with a highly strategic and automated workload. Seventy-nine percent of CPOs describe 2026 as a more challenging year, while 75% expect to outperform their 2025 results. That tension, between pressure and confidence, runs through everything.

Three themes tie this edition together.

The first is the execution gap. Whether it is AI deployment, contract risk management, supplier performance tracking, or supply market intelligence, organisations have built the case but not the capability. Process debt, data fragmentation, and governance inertia slow progress at every turn. The tools are available. The operating models to use them well are not.

The second is the cost of passivity. Late payments are draining cash from finance teams. Contract auto-renewals go unnoticed. Geopolitical clauses go unrevised. Preferred supplier programmes exist on paper but are not enforced. The cost of inaction is not theoretical; it is measurable, and the numbers in this month's reports are uncomfortable reading.

The third is the timing problem. Several reports this month argue that procurement intervenes too late, whether in, AI adoption, or contract lifecycle management. By the time a risk becomes visible, many of the options to address it have already closed. The organisations gaining ground are the ones building their engagement upstream, before decisions lock in.

Beroe/Hackett - Supply Market Intelligence: From Insight to Impact

Supply market intelligence delivers better outcomes than almost any other investment procurement can make. Returns can exceed two hundred dollars in savings for every dollar spent. Incremental cost savings average 1.5 percentage points above baseline. The ROI case is not complicated.

The adoption picture is. Forty-two percent of organisations report that supply market intelligence is either not implemented or entirely ad hoc. Only 5% have advanced end-to-end capabilities. The barriers are not a mystery. Manual and inefficient processes are cited by 49% of respondents. Technology integration challenges by 46%. Weak data analysis capability by 45%. Data silos, inaccurate data, and unreliable data sources each above 44%.

What the data shows is a function drowning in the mechanics of the work rather than building the intelligence capability that would change the work's outcomes. Talent constraints rank far lower as a barrier at 31%. The problem is not people. It is process and architecture.

The value of SMI extends beyond cost reduction. Better negotiations. More confident supplier selection. Stronger risk mitigation before disruption arrives rather than after. Increased credibility with the business when procurement shows up with market data rather than opinion.

Hybrid models, combining internal category expertise with third-party intelligence, consistently outperform either approach alone. If your organisation relies on a single source, you are leaving most of that return on the table.

WorldCC - Geopolitical Disruption: Commercial Paralysis

Across nine sectors and seven regions, the mean commercial impact score for geopolitical disruption sits at 2.76 out of 5. That is the score of an organisation that feels the pressure but cannot convert concern into action. Thirty-nine percent have no formal or only ad hoc geopolitical risk governance. Only 15% have board-level oversight with escalation triggers. Thirty-five percent made no significant contract clause changes in the past twelve months.

The most actively revised clause is price escalation, revised by 47% of respondents. Force majeure and alternative sourcing follow at 35% each. The pattern suggests organisations are reacting to cost rather than building genuine flexibility into their commercial relationships.

Three structural problems explain the inertia. The unlocatable risk problem: organisations cannot calculate the cost of disruption because they do not know where it will land. The fragmented offset problem: the costs and risk buffers sit across functions that do not share data with each other. The circular resistance problem: every step one party takes to increase resilience generates resistance from counterparties who see it as a cost imposition.

Sixty-three percent of sell-side disputes are resolved through renegotiation rather than formal claims. It tells you where the real commercial value exists. The organisations making progress are not writing tougher clauses. They are connecting governance, pricing, and relationship management into a coherent commercial response.

Agiloft/Art of Procurement - From Fire Drill to Foresight

Every organisation is built on contracts. Most organisations manage those contracts reactively. This paper, , describes the cost of that approach and what a more deliberate one looks like.

Research suggests most organisations lose between 5% and 9% of revenue to missed or poorly managed contractual obligations. The most common causes are quiet ones. Data handling language that has drifted from current business practice. Pricing clauses that favour suppliers because nobody built in adequate controls. Regulatory obligations that were compliant when the contract was signed three years ago but may not be today.

Aberdeen Group research finds that 42% of enterprises cite risk mitigation as a top driver for improving contract management. That is a recognition that passive contract management has a measurable cost.

The practical fix described in this paper is not primarily a technology deployment. It is a process and workflow problem. Microsoft's contract team manages thousands of agreements with two attorneys supporting all of procurement. The answer is playbooks that encode risk posture, intake processes that route contracts to the right reviewers, and alerts going out ninety days before any auto-renewal triggers.

The paper's clearest advice for organisations just starting: centralise contracts, build an intake workflow, and extract a small set of high-value data points before expanding to broader automation. Overreach early is the most common implementation failure.

Foundry - State of the CIO Study 2026

Six hundred and sixty-two IT leaders and 249 line-of-business respondents participated in Foundry's 25th annual CIO study.

The top CEO priority for IT leaders in 2026 is to research and implement AI products and projects, cited by 27% of respondents and consistent with last year at 26%. Accelerating AI-driven innovation and applications is the number one business initiative, earmarked by 39% of CIOs as a driver of IT investment. Generative AI (67%), machine learning (66%), and agentic AI (65%) lead the technology investment list.

Seventy-four percent of respondents say AI is already or is beginning to reshape operations. The CIO role is evolving at pace. Eighty-two percent of IT leaders are tasked with researching and evaluating AI additions to the enterprise technology stack, and 79% say the CIO is working more closely with line-of-business on AI applications than in prior years.

The barriers are familiar. Forty percent of respondents cite lack of in-house AI expertise as a critical challenge. Thirty-two percent point to a lack of clear ROI metrics. Thirty-one percent say corporate AI strategy lacks clarity. Only 19% say AI initiatives have met or exceeded their ROI goals so far.

The CIO is increasingly the point for enterprise AI decisions. Their agenda in 2026 is dominated by agentic AI deployment, cybersecurity, and building the governance structures that let AI operate at enterprise scale. That is your conversation to have.

Ardent Partners - AI Rising 2026: The State of Procurement AI

Fifty-eight percent of the market are now actively using or piloting AI. Ardent Partners estimates that by the end of 2026, more procurement teams will be actively using AI than have an eProcurement system in place. That comparison is not trivial. eProcurement took two decades to reach near-universal adoption. AI is moving on a different timeline entirely.

Cost savings is the top priority for 75% of CPOs, a proportion that has almost exactly doubled since 2022. Supply risk management sits second at 48%. Digital transformation and AI deployment are functionally inseparable now, each cited by 31% as top three priorities, and together representing a single transformation agenda.

The CPO challenge is a familiar squeeze: budget constraints cited by 53% as a top-three barrier, combined with misaligned processes and fragmented systems at 37%. The function is being asked to deliver more value with the same or fewer resources while simultaneously executing an AI transformation.

Ardent's maturity curve shows 22% of organisations actively deploying AI, 35% piloting, and 32% still in exploration. Only 1% describe AI as incorporated into core processes at enterprise level. The direction is consistent and, as the report argues, irreversible. What is not consistent is the speed. The organisations that get the sequencing right, data first, governance second, deployment third, are the ones building durable advantage.

SMARTnership - How AI Transforms Negotiation Work

Negotiation is where procurement decisions turn into results. It is also one of the last areas of business performance that is not systematically tracked, measured, or supported by connected technology. This report, based on a study of negotiation professionals across procurement, sales, legal, finance, and executive leadership, describes the gap in uncomfortable detail.

Forty-two percent of deal value may be left unrealised. One study cohort of 47 professionals spent over 27,500 hours per year on negotiation-related work, a loaded cost of $5.94 million annually. That is the invisible operating cost of managing negotiations the way most organisations currently manage them.

Seventy-five percent of negotiators see AI as useful for workflow pieces such as research, drafting, and contract summarisation. Only 20% use AI in live preparation or review. Just 5% have a connected workflow spanning the full negotiation lifecycle. The tools exist across functions: CRM in sales, CLM in legal, ERP in operations. What does not exist in most organisations is a connected system for negotiation itself.

The distinction the report draws between generic AI assistance and negotiation-grade AI matters. Professionals are confident using AI for isolated tasks. They are significantly less confident using it as a decision system. Negotiation requires judgment, context, value logic, and trust awareness that generic tools do not yet provide well.

The real shift demanded of senior leaders is not technical. It is conceptual: from seeing AI as a writing assistant to seeing it as a structured intelligence system for one of the highest-value activities the organisation undertakes.

BCG - Scaling Agentic AI in Tech Procurement

Two hundred or more CIOs, procurement leaders, and specialist tech buyers across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific participated in this BCG survey on agentic AI in technology procurement.

Internal operational benefits appear earlier than external supplier-facing commercial benefits. Production deployments generate much stronger returns than pilots. Combining technology with capability building, process redesign, and governance reports significantly stronger outcomes than technology deployment alone.

Six use cases were studied: vendor discovery, RFP generation, contract analysis, spend analysis, risk monitoring, and supplier performance management. The top reported benefits are speed, throughput, and reduction in manual effort. Less frequently reported are broader supplier coverage and stronger negotiation outcomes. AI is accelerating existing processes before it is changing their outcomes.

One automotive manufacturer redesigned its entire procurement lifecycle around AI rather than simply automating existing tasks. The result converted productivity gains into negotiation uplift and EBIT contribution worth more than ten times the internal efficiency value alone. That multiplier only appears when process redesign precedes technology deployment.

The barriers are significant. Data foundations: approximately one-third cite the cost of data preparation as a blocker. Legacy system integration: nearly half cite ERP and P2P integration difficulty. Governance: 71% cite trust in autonomous decision-making as the biggest organisational barrier, with 57% citing regulatory uncertainty. The technology capability is ahead of the governance structures needed to use it well.

As always reach out to discuss more, and always happy to hear your thoughts!

entry.title: Gordon Donovan: Procurement’s Next Era Will Be Defined by Outcomes, Resilience, and AI
entry.content:
🚀Gordon Donovan: Procurement’s Next Era Will Be Defined by Outcomes, Resilience, and AI

🎙️ In a special episode of The Future of Procurement recorded at the World Procurement Congress ahead of SAP Connect 2026, SAP VP of Research - Procurement Gordon Donovan sat down with three leaders shaping the future of healthcare procurement: Richard Evans, Executive Commercial Director of Supply Chain at NHS Supply Chain, Sirsij Peshin, Chief Procurement Officer (CPO) and Global Source-to-Pay Lead at Pfizer, and Alan Rankin, Chief Procurement Officer(CPO) at Moderna. Despite representing very different organizations, their perspectives converged around a common reality: procurement is entering a new era where resilience, intelligence, and business outcomes matter more than ever.

🎯Procurement Is Shifting From Process to Outcomes

💡One of the strongest themes Gordon uncovered was procurement’s evolution from a process-driven function to an outcome-driven one. Richard Evans described how NHS Supply Chain responded to critical supply disruptions with a singular focus: ensuring patients received care and clinicians had the products they needed. In those moments, success was not measured by adherence to process but by continuity of care and operational outcomes.

📈Gordon highlighted that this mindset is becoming increasingly common across procurement. Compliance and governance remain essential, but leading organizations are starting with the outcome they need to achieve and then designing processes that support it, rather than allowing process to dictate the result.

🛡️ Resilience Has Become Business as Usual

🌍Across each discussion, resilience emerged not as a project, but as a foundational capability. Evans shared how investments in supply chain intelligence and visibility into tier-two and tier-three suppliers have enabled NHS Supply Chain to proactively manage risks before they impact healthcare delivery.

🏭Moderna's Alan Rankin echoed this perspective, discussing the company’s approach to building localized manufacturing and supply capabilities through partnerships with governments. These investments are designed to ensure critical healthcare products remain available during future disruptions.

🔍Gordon's key observation was that resilience is no longer something procurement organizations add on. It is increasingly embedded into how they buy, manage suppliers, and make decisions every day.

🤝Supplier Relationships Are Strategic Assets

🌟Sirsij Peshin emphasized that procurement's success depends on the strength of its supplier ecosystem. At Pfizer, long-standing partnerships enabled collaboration, innovation, and responsiveness at scale, particularly during periods of global disruption. Importantly, he stressed that value comes not only from major strategic suppliers but also from smaller partners that play vital roles across the supply network.

🔗Gordon connected this insight to a broader trend across the profession: procurement leaders are increasingly focused on understanding and managing entire supplier ecosystems rather than simply managing contracts and spend categories.

🤖AI Is Redefining How Procurement Creates Value

🚀AI was central to all three conversations, but not simply as a technology topic. Gordon found that leading organizations are focused on redesigning work itself. Sirsij described a future where AI helps identify issues before they become business problems, enabling "biopsies rather than autopsies." The goal is to automate routine work, augment decision-making, and allow procurement professionals to spend more time creating value.

📊Rankin added that as software becomes more commoditized, data will become the true source of competitive advantage. Organizations that can structure, govern, and leverage data effectively will be best positioned to capitalize on AI’s potential.

⚙️For Gordon, the conversation is rapidly shifting from whether procurement should adopt AI to how the function should be redesigned around AI-enabled workflows and decision-making.

💭Gordon’s Biggest Takeaway: What Will Procurement Stop Doing?

✨Reflecting on all three conversations, Gordon identified one question that every procurement leader should be asking: What are we going to stop doing? As procurement teams embrace automation, AI, and expanding strategic responsibilities, they cannot continue adding work without removing activities that no longer create value.

📌Gordon also pointed to another important lesson from Richard Evans. The value of risk management is often invisible. The true measure of resilience is not how organizations react when a disruption occurs, but how effectively they prevent disruptions from occurring in the first place. When stakeholders trust procurement and remain confident in the supply chain, that trust becomes a powerful indicator of success.

🔮Looking Ahead

🚀Gordon’s conversations with NHS Supply Chain, Pfizer, and Moderna paint a clear picture of where procurement is heading. Resilience is becoming standard practice. Supplier ecosystems are growing in importance. AI is transforming operating models. And perhaps most importantly, procurement is increasingly measured by the outcomes it delivers rather than the processes it follows.

🌟As organizations navigate uncertainty and technological change, the opportunity for procurement has never been greater. The leaders shaping the future are not waiting for disruption to happen. They are proactively building more resilient supply chains, deeper supplier partnerships, and smarter operating models today.

👉What are you doing to prepare your procurement organization for an AI-native future? More importantly, what will you stop doing to make room for the work that delivers the greatest value? Join the conversation, connect with Gordon Donovan on LinkedIn, and share your perspective on the trends shaping procurement’s next chapter.

entry.title: Introducing the Service Procurement Agent for SAP S/4HANA
entry.content:
The Next Evolution of Service Procurement Automation

Service procurement teams spend a significant amount of time manually reviewing supplier service confirmations, validating supporting documents, comparing them against purchase orders, creating Service Entry Sheets (SES), and resolving mismatches before services can be accepted and invoiced.

As organizations continue to scale operations, this manual effort becomes increasingly challenging, often resulting in processing delays, compliance risks, and increased operational costs.

We're excited to share a preview of an upcoming Service Procurement Agent for SAP S/4HANA , an AI-powered agent designed to transform how organizations process service procurement transactions by intelligently creating Service Entry Sheets from supplier documents while keeping procurement professionals in complete control.

Business Challenge

Consider a typical scenario:

A supplier sends an email containing:

  • Service completion documentation
  • Supporting PDF attachments
  • Service reports
  • Invoices or service confirmations

A purchaser user must:

  1. Open and review the email.
  2. Download and analyze attachments.
  3. Locate the corresponding purchase order in SAP S/4HANA.
  4. Verify quantities, pricing, service descriptions, and dates.
  5. Create the Service Entry Sheet.
  6. Resolve discrepancies through back-and-forth communication.
  7. Track processing status across multiple suppliers.

When repeated hundreds of times per month, this becomes a highly manual and repetitive process.

Meet the Service Procurement Agent

The upcoming SAP S/4HANA Service Procurement Agent leverages AI to automate the end-to-end Service Entry Sheet creation process using supplier emails and supporting documents as input.

The agent can:

✅Read supplier emails

✅Extract information from PDF attachments and service documents

✅Match documents to corresponding SAP S/4HANA purchase orders

✅Validate service quantities, rates, and descriptions

✅Automatically create Service Entry Sheets

✅Detect discrepancies and exceptions

✅Recommend resolution actions

✅Keep users informed through summary notifications

Intelligent Document Understanding

The agent goes beyond simple document extraction.

Using advanced document intelligence, it understands:

  • Service descriptions
  • Work completion reports
  • Resource effort summaries
  • Quantity confirmations
  • Service periods
  • Supplier references
  • Purchase order references

It can correlate information across multiple documents and identify the most relevant purchase order and service lines within SAP S/4HANA.

Example

Supplier PDF

  • Maintenance Services
  • 120 Hours Completed
  • Service Period: May 1-31

SAP S/4HANA Purchase Order

  • Planned Maintenance Services
  • Approved Quantity: 120 Hours

The agent validates the alignment and automatically creates the Service Entry Sheet with confidence.

Built-In Anomaly Detection

A key differentiator is the agent's ability to identify exceptions before creating a Service Entry Sheet.

The agent continuously compares supplier-submitted information against SAP purchasing data and business rules.

Examples of anomalies detected

Quantity Mismatch

Purchase Order:

  • 100 hours approved

Supplier Document:

  • 120 hours claimed

The agent flags the discrepancy before posting.

Price Variance

Purchase Order:

  • $50 per hour

Supplier Document:

  • $60 per hour

The agent identifies the variance and prevents incorrect posting.

Missing References

  • Invalid PO number
  • Missing service line information
  • Expired contract references

Duplicate Submissions

The agent can detect previously processed service confirmations and avoid duplicate SES creation.

Human-in-the-Loop Resolution

Not every situation should be fully automated.

When discrepancies are detected, the Service Procurement Agent automatically brings the appropriate business user into the process.

The user receives:

  • A summary of detected issues
  • Impact analysis
  • Underlying supporting documents
  • Recommended resolution options

Example Resolution Recommendation

Issue Detected:

Supplier submitted 120 hours against a PO with 100 approved hours.

Agent Recommendation:

Option 1: Create SES for approved 100 hours and route remaining 20 hours for approval.

Option 2: Request PO amendment before SES creation.

Option 3: Reject submission and notify supplier.

The final decision remains with the business user, ensuring compliance and governance.

Processing Multiple Documents at Scale

Service organizations often receive large volumes of supplier submissions daily.

The Service Procurement Agent can process multiple:

  • Emails
  • PDF attachments

in a single execution cycle.

Rather than requiring users to process each service confirmation individually, the agent works through the complete document queue and automatically classifies outcomes into:

Successfully Processed

  • SES created
  • SES send for Approval
  • Reference documents linked

Requires Review

  • Quantity mismatches
  • Pricing deviations
  • Missing information
  • Validation failures

Failed Processing

  • Unsupported documents
  • Missing purchase order references
  • System exceptions

Transparent Outcome Communication

At the end of processing, the agent generates a comprehensive summary email to stakeholders.

Sample Summary Email

Subject: Service Procurement Agent Processing Summary

Dear Procurement Team,

Today's service document processing has completed successfully.

Processing Statistics

  • Total Supplier Submissions Received: 125
  • Service Entry Sheets Automatically Posted: 104
  • Submitted for Human Review: 16
  • Failed Processing: 5

Top Exceptions

  • Quantity Variance: 8
  • Missing PO Reference: 4
  • Price Mismatch: 3
  • Invalid Service Line: 1

Please review the exceptions dashboard for further action.

Regards,

Service Procurement Agent

This ensures complete transparency and operational visibility without requiring manual status tracking.

Business Benefits

Organizations adopting the Service Procurement Agent can expect:

Increased Efficiency

Reduce manual SES creation effort and accelerate service acceptance processes.

Improved Accuracy

Minimize data entry errors through intelligent document validation.

Better Compliance

Ensure alignment between supplier submissions and approved purchasing agreements.

Faster Exception Resolution

Leverage AI-generated recommendations to resolve discrepancies quickly.

Enhanced User Productivity

Allow procurement teams to focus on high-value activities rather than administrative processing.

Looking Ahead

The SAP S/4HANA Service Procurement Agent represents the next step toward autonomous procurement operations, where AI assists users by handling repetitive tasks, proactively identifying risks, and intelligently collaborating with humans when decisions are required.

By combining document intelligence, anomaly detection, human-in-the-loop approvals, and large-scale processing capabilities, organizations can streamline service procurement while maintaining control, compliance, and transparency.

The future of service procurement is not just automated. It's intelligent, collaborative, and proactive.

entry.title: Taking Procurement from Gatekeeper to Advisory with Mitch Myers
entry.content:
From Gatekeeper to Strategic Advisor: Rethinking Value in Procurement Transformation

🔄Transformation rarely follows a straight line. Organizations can implement new platforms, redesign processes, and introduce new capabilities, yet still struggle to answer the most important question: What business value did we actually create? In a recent discussion, Mitch Myers, Director, Solution and Value Advisory, SAP Finance & Spend, drew on more than 25 years of SAP technology, consulting, procurement, and value advisory experience to explore why successful transformation requires organizations to look beyond implementation and make value the guiding principle for change. 

🎧LISTEN:  https://pod.link/1764078646/episode/ODljMjcxYTYtYjM2NC00ODk0LTgxYTgtOWYyZGU1YjVhZGMx 

🎯Process improvement is not the same as value creation

💡One of the strongest messages from the conversation is deceptively simple: improving a process does not automatically create meaningful business value. Transformation teams can easily devote disproportionate attention to complaints, incremental refinements, or achieving a theoretically perfect process. The danger is effectively reversing the 80/20 rule, spending 80% of the effort pursuing 20% of the potential value.

📊Instead, organizations should evaluate improvements through a value lens. Does a proposed change generate measurable savings? Improve compliance? Increase efficiency? Reduce risk? Enable a more valuable capability? Those questions can help leaders allocate limited transformation resources toward outcomes that truly move the business forward.

🗺️ Think roadmap, not finish line

🌱Cloud transformation also challenges the idea that an implementation is ever truly “finished.” Rather than continually polishing one area in pursuit of perfection, Mitch Myers advocates time-boxing priorities and establishing a roadmap of what comes next. Organizations can capture the majority of available value, establish a solid foundation, then move to the next significant opportunity.

🔁This is particularly relevant in cloud environments, where capabilities continue to evolve. Transformation becomes a cycle of adoption, measurement, innovation, and optimization rather than a one-time event. That also makes ongoing services and support increasingly important. The goal is not simply to deploy technology, but to help users mature with it and continually realize more value from their investment.

📏Measure outcomes, not activity

📈Another critical lesson is to distinguish activity metrics from value metrics. Measuring spend flowing through catalogs, the number of contracts processed, or the volume of transactions may demonstrate adoption, but those measures alone do not prove business impact. Mitch Myers argues that organizations need to connect those activities to outcomes such as increased compliance, reduced costs, improved efficiency, or other quantifiable benefits.

🤝Building a credible business case is equally important. Instead of simply presenting an outside-in ROI estimate and expecting stakeholders to accept it, transformation leaders should bring stakeholders into the process, test assumptions against organizational realities, and construct an inside-out view of achievable value. The projected return may decrease as assumptions are challenged, but its credibility and organizational ownership can increase.

👥Successful transformation requires three P’s

🧩 Technology alone cannot transform an organization. Mitch Myers frames successful transformation around people, process, and platforms. If any one of the three is missing, even sophisticated technology can fail to deliver the intended result.

🌐This becomes especially important when organizations introduce standardized processes across different functions, regions, and cultures. What looks clearly superior from a technology perspective may still face resistance if employees cannot understand how the change creates value for them. The case for change therefore needs to connect enterprise objectives with the everyday experience of users.

🤖AI is accelerating the journey toward autonomous operations

🚀The forward-looking implications are significant. Mitch Myers sees AI agents creating a credible path toward increasingly autonomous procurement and finance operations. Activities involving moving, connecting, monitoring, and analyzing data can increasingly be handled by intelligent systems, freeing professionals to focus on higher-value work.

🧠 That shift may fundamentally reshape procurement’s role. Procurement historically operated as a gatekeeper, establishing controls and deciding how purchases could happen. It has increasingly become a business partner, collaborating with functions to improve spending decisions. The next evolution is procurement as a strategic advisor, proactively bringing intelligence, insights, and opportunities to the business.

🌟The future is about value, not just technology

💬The ultimate measure of transformation is not whether a system went live or a process changed. It is whether the organization created measurable value and built the capacity to create more.

🔭As AI, cloud platforms, finance, and procurement become more interconnected, successful organizations will continuously ask: Where is our next source of value, and are our people, processes, and platforms aligned to capture it? That mindset could be what finally moves procurement from a function the business has to involve to an advisor the business wants at the table.

entry.title: Curiosity, Resilience and AI: What Leading CPOs Are Building Now
entry.content:
Curiosity, Resilience and AI: What Leading CPOs Are Building Now

Insights from The Future of Procurement podcast:  https://pod.link/1764078646

🎙️ Procurement’s future is not waiting on the horizon. It is taking shape in today’s decisions about artificial intelligence, supply resilience, talent, and business value. In a special episode of The Future of Procurement, Gordon Donovan, Vice President Research – Procurement & External Workforce at SAP, brings together perspectives from the chief procurement leaders of Nestlé, Kraft Heinz and Heineken. Their organizations face different category dynamics, yet their messages converge around a powerful idea: procurement can turn disruption into advantage when technology is paired with judgment, curiosity and commercial confidence.

Curiosity is becoming a core procurement capability

🔎 Across all three conversations, curiosity emerged as more than a desirable behavior. It is becoming an operating requirement. Procurement teams must continually scan geopolitical developments, weather patterns, commodity markets, tariffs, supplier conditions, and new technologies. The professionals who experiment, ask better questions and challenge assumptions are better positioned to identify threats early and uncover opportunities that a narrow, transactional view would miss.

💡 This matters because volatility is now persistent rather than exceptional. A change in crop conditions can affect cocoa or coffee availability. A tariff decision can alter the economics of a sourcing origin overnight. Curiosity enables teams to connect these external signals with category strategies, product requirements, and the company’s growth agenda. For leaders, the practical implication is clear: create structured opportunities for people to explore AI, test scenarios and share what they learn, rather than leaving adoption to a few enthusiasts.

AI should amplify judgment, not put procurement on autopilot

🤖 The CPOs described meaningful AI progress in productivity use cases, including contract summarization, data cleansing, planning, content creation and process guidance. The next horizon is more ambitious: agentic workflows, hands-free procurement experiences, and AI support for category strategy. These capabilities can reduce transactional effort and give professionals more capacity for supplier relationships, market intelligence, and strategic decision-making.

⚠️ But the episode also draws an important boundary. AI output cannot become an instruction that people accept without scrutiny. Contracts, sourcing choices and category recommendations still require business context, critical evaluation, and accountability. “Human in the lead” is therefore not resistance to automation. It is a design principle: let technology assemble information, surface patterns and accelerate routine work, while skilled people test the logic and own the decision.

Resilience and cost are not opposing choices

🛡️ The traditional debate frames resilience as an added cost: dual sources, inventory buffers, alternate origins and qualified backup sites all require investment. The leaders in this episode offer a more strategic view. The real question is where resilience produces the greatest return relative to risk and competition. A company does not need every item dual sourced. It needs a fact-based view of criticality, exposure, recovery options, and the commercial consequences of interruption.

📈 That leads to targeted resilience. Teams can pre-qualify multiple supplier locations, develop local and imported options, adapt formulations where appropriate, and document contingency actions before a crisis. Some preparation costs little until activated, yet it can materially improve response speed. The competitive benefit is not merely avoiding disruption. It is absorbing volatility more smoothly than peers and protecting availability, margins and customer preference.

Procurement value must connect to business strategy

🤝 Cost discipline remains essential, but world-class procurement communicates value in the language of the enterprise. Savings can fund brand investment and growth. Supplier partnerships can accelerate innovation and sustainability. Better contracts can protect flexibility and reduce risk. Strong market insight can inform pricing, planning, and investment decisions. The function earns influence when it understands the business strategy, builds confidence with senior stakeholders, and speaks up with a clear point of view.

🌱 The talent model must evolve with that mandate. As shared services, robotics and AI absorb more transactional work, teams will need stronger business partnering, storytelling, influencing and strategic judgment. Leaders should reinvest a portion of technology-enabled efficiency into capability building, ensuring that a potentially smaller organization is also more skilled, externally aware and effective.

A leadership call to action

🚀 Procurement leaders should ask three questions now:

  1. Are we deliberately building curiosity?
  2. Have we defined where AI assists and where people must decide?
  3. Are resilience investments tied to critical business outcomes and competitive position?

The organizations that answer these questions with discipline will be better equipped to convert uncertainty into sustainable value.
